parakeet: When someone wants to critique Christianity's harms and reduce its public influence, they're almost never dealing with one fixed thing. They're dealing with a religion that can constantly reframe itself through different theological frameworks, denominational structures, moral vocabularies, and public postures. That means critique is harder because Christianity is not just a set of beliefs, it's a highly adaptive interpretive ecosystem. First, Christianity can evade criticism by shifting frameworks. So even when a critique lands against one expression, the broader tradition often survives by saying that's not real Christianity, or that's just one version. The internal diversity becomes a defense shield. Critics may point to misogyny, homophobia, authoritarianism, purity culture, apocalyptic fear, anti-scientific thinking, or political domination. But Christians can respond by saying those harms are not intrinsic to Christianity itself, only to bad interpretations. That makes systemic critique much harder because the religion can keep disowning its own outcomes. Because Christianity has so many frameworks available, it can speak in soft moral language publicly while drawing on older theological authority structures underneath. That makes it difficult for critics to explain the danger because the most visible version is not always the most operative version. Once Christianity has thousands of denominations and dozens of theological frameworks, every critique can be met with a counterexample. Those rebuttals may be true at one level, but they can derail the deeper issue, which is that Christianity contains enough eternal elasticity to repeatedly generate these harms while also producing enough softer expressions to protect itself from wholesale moral indictment.
